Solution 2 and Solution 3 both have final answers that I can refute, and Solution 1's answer is the only one I can't rule out, though its proof is incomplete.

**Solution 3 (2/3)** claims every weak Sidon set has h(A) ≥ ⌈2n/3⌉. The Fibonacci-type set A = {0, 1, 2, 4, 7, 12, 20, 33, 54, 88} is weak Sidon (I checked all 45 pairwise sums, and they are distinct). Its 3-APs are the 8 triples {0,1,2}, {0,2,4}, {1,4,7}, {2,7,12}, {4,12,20}, {7,20,33}, {12,33,54}, {20,54,88}, with index edges E1={0,1,2}, E2={0,2,3}, E3={1,3,4}, E4={2,4,5}, E5={3,5,6}, E6={4,6,7}, E7={5,7,8}, E8={6,8,9}. A 3-vertex transversal would need either two degree-3 vertices with disjoint edge sets plus a degree-2 vertex, or three degree-3 vertices with only one shared edge incidence. Checking both cases rules these out, so the minimum transversal is 4 and h(A) = 6 < ⌈20/3⌉ = 7. The Solution 3 lower-bound step is therefore false. Its cluster construction also only gives an upper bound of 2/3, and the Fibonacci family appears to have asymptotic density 3/5, which is below 2/3.

**Solution 2 (3/5)** has an upper-bound construction that checks out at small n (n = 5 gives 3, n = 10 gives 6). But its lower bound is asserted rather than proved ("careful analysis shows this is tight"), so 3/5 is at best an upper bound on the limit. Nothing in the argument rules out weak Sidon sets with smaller h.

**Solution 1 (0)** has a valid lower bound: h(A) = Ω(n^{2/3}). Its counting argument is sound: each of at most n−2 APs lies in C(n−3, t−3) of the t-subsets, so some t-subset is AP-free once t(t−1)(t−2) < n(n−1). But this only gives g(n)/n ≥ 0, not g(n)/n → 0. The missing piece is a construction with h = o(n), which Solution 1 does not provide. I believe the known answer may be 0, but I cannot confirm that from the reasoning given, so this choice is tentative.

CHOICE: 1
